articles.title: Aditya-L1 reveals asymmetric expansion of solar eruptions - OrissaPOST
articles.content: New Delhi: India’s first space-based solar observatory, Aditya-L1, has helped scientists uncover new details about the behaviour of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) beneficial for space-weather studies and thereby affecting satellites and communication networks, an official statement said Tuesday. The statement from the Ministry of Science & Technology said observations revealed for the first time that these massive solar eruptions do not expand uniformly as previously assumed. Also Read Sonowal announces Rs 1,500-crore cruise terminal in Puri 7 hours ago Indian seafarer killed in attack on ship near Oman 8 hours ago These differences in CME expansion can affect its speed as it travels towards Earth, causing space-weather disturbances. Researchers from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) combined observations from the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC) aboard Aditya-L1 with data from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and three-dimensional modelling to reconstruct the full 3-D geometry and dynamics of a CME. “The asymmetric shape of an early CME can have important implications for how it interacts with the solar wind and experiences drag during its propagation through the heliosphere. Such effects can influence the CME’s speed and, ultimately, its arrival time at Earth”, said Jayant Joshi of IIA and a co-author of the study published in Astrophysical Journal Letters. Aditya L 1 satellite launched in September 2023 is now operational at the Sun–Earth L1 point, providing continuous observations of the Sun. It carries 7 payloads, of which the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), the primary payload, is an internally occulted coronagraph designed to observe the solar corona simultaneously in various modes. The model was used to test how the CME’s orientation and uneven sideways expansion could produce the spectral structures observed by VELC. The researchers plan to use this technique on other CMEs, to reconstruct their motion without relying entirely on multi-viewpoint imaging from telescopes in space. This complementarity is particularly valuable in the lower corona, where CMEs evolve rapidly, and their motion along the line of sight cannot be obtained from imaging alone, the statement noted. articles.title: Rajkumari wins India's first wushu medal at Youth Olympics - Hindustan Times
articles.content: Rajkumari wins India's first wushu medal at Youth Olympics She won bronze in women’s changquan combined wushu event Published on: Nov 3, 2026, 23:56:32 IST By HT Correspondent Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link Rajkumari Lanchenbi Chanu won a historic bronze medal for India in wushu at the Youth Olympic Games 2026 in Dakar, Senegal on Tuesday, taking the country's medal tally to three. Rajkumari Lanchenbi Chanu Rajkumari won bronze in the women’s changquan combined wushu event. She scored 8.723 in gunshu and 9.316 in changquan for a combined total of 18.039, finishing third. Egypt’s Sondos Sonbol claimed the gold medal with a total score of 18.660 while Venezuela’s Valeria Frannerys Dudamel Alvarado took silver (18.199). This is the first time that wushu is part of Youth Olympics programme as a medal sport. The changquan combined event is a routine-based (taolu) wushu discipline that combines a bare-handed routine and a weapon routine. The scores of both are added for a final total. The competition spanned three days and the top eight qualified for the final round. Rajkumari placed second among 12 athletes in the preliminary stage with a total of 17.982. Rajkumari, who hails from Manipur, was the only Indian in wushu and displayed remarkable grit to win a medal. This was India's third medal at the Dakar Youth Olympics. On Monday, Khushbu Rajakbhai Darjada won silver in the women’s judo (63kg category) and swimmer Dhinidhi Desinghu bagged bronze in the women’s 100m freestyle. "Rajkumari Lanchenbi Chanu has created history for Indian wushu by winning first-ever medal in the sport at the Youth Olympics. It was possible because of her hard work and determination and the hard work of coached and support staff," the Wushu Association of India said in a statement.
